title: The Richest Man in Babylon
description: Fifteen ideas from Clason's Babylon parables, read with care in daily Indian money life.
author: codex

topic.title: The Richest Man in Babylon
topic.description: Read old money tales with clear eyes and daily examples.

book.title: The Richest Man in Babylon
book.author: George S. Clason
book.edition: 1926 parables; Wikisource transcription of the 90-page 1926 scan, The Richest Man In Babylon
book.blurb: Old tales ask how we save, spend, lend, and plan. We test their ideas in life today.

concepts.title: Keep a share
concepts.hook: Salary lands, then bills arrive. Arkad asks what stays with the earner. What if the bills leave no room?
concepts.rule: Arkad's first cure is to set aside one coin in ten. That is a story rule, not a rate that fits all homes. Food, rent, and debt can use up the pay.

claims.text: In Seven Cures, Arkad says, ‘For each ten coins I put in, to spend but nine.’ He uses this as his first cure.
Arkad treats one tenth as a rule for all earners. A US study finds that low pay and fixed costs can block a cash buffer.
SEBI says savings can build an emergency fund for unexpected costs such as medical bills or business loss. The share a home can save depends on its income and expenses.

items.stem: At a Delhi office, pay arrives by bank transfer. What part of Arkad's tale can the worker test?

options.text: See what stays after pay day.
options.feedback: The first cure asks what part of earnings remains in the purse.

options.text: Treat the full pay as free cash.
options.feedback: Bills still draw on the pay, so the full sum is not spare cash.

items.stem: A family uses almost all its pay for rent and food. Why can one tenth be hard to keep?

options.feedback: The study notes that fixed costs and low income can limit cash set aside.

options.text: The family has no will to save.
options.feedback: That judges the family and skips the cost of rent and food.

items.stem: A UPI budget shows a small spare sum after bills. What may a saved part do over time?

options.feedback: A small reserve may help meet a sudden cost if it stays in reach.
Savings can help meet a bill, but they do not erase the bill.

items.stem: A shop has a slow month and a repair bill. Which reading of the first cure is fair?

options.text: The amount kept may vary with costs.
options.feedback: The book gives a fixed share, but real cash flow can change by month.

options.text: The shop can owe rent to keep one tenth.
options.feedback: The story's rule does not make rent or repair costs go away.

items.stem: A cousin says one tenth is a test of virtue. Which reply fits the evidence?

options.feedback: Income and fixed bills shape the space a person has to save.

options.text: A low rate shows poor character.
options.feedback: That turns a cash limit into blame and ignores the study's findings.

items.stem: In the keep-a-share cure, how many coins stay in the purse if nine of ten are spent?

options.feedback: The tale sets one aside and uses nine out of ten.
Nine is the part spent in the tale, not the part kept.

misconceptions.name: Pay equals spare cash
misconceptions.correction: Bills take part of pay. The first cure asks what can remain after needs.

misconceptions.name: One rate fits all
misconceptions.correction: A fixed share can be hard when pay is low or bills are high.

steps.title: Name the kept part

hook.stem: If ten coins come in, what does Arkad keep?

options.feedback: One coin is his kept share.
Nine coins are for use.

steps.teach: Arkad keeps one coin from ten because he wants his purse to grow. The tale starts with what stays, not just what comes in.

example.feedback: That is the part the first cure asks us to notice.

guided.stem: A worker notes cash left after pay day. What is the tale's key question?
guided.hint: Think of the end of the month.

options.feedback: The cure starts with a share kept.
The pay alone does not show what stayed.

steps.takeaway: Notice the share that stays.

steps.title: Let cash meet a shock

hook.stem: A sudden clinic bill arrives. What can spare cash do?

options.feedback: Cash in reach can help with a shock.
A reserve cannot prevent illness.

steps.teach: A cash cushion can help because a surprise bill needs money at once. The sum that can stay aside depends on the home's bills.

example.feedback: The reserve helps meet the cost rather than remove it.

guided.stem: A train trip is urgent. What can money in reach help with?
guided.hint: Think of what is due soon.

options.feedback: A reserve may help pay a sudden fare.
Cash does not make travel free.

steps.takeaway: Spare cash can soften a sudden cost.

steps.title: Question the fixed rate

hook.stem: Can each home keep the same share each month?

options.feedback: Fixed bills can leave very little spare cash.
Pay and basic needs differ by home.

steps.teach: Arkad's rule is one tenth. It is too broad because low pay and fixed bills can block saving.

example.feedback: The fixed rent leaves a small share, even with care.

guided.stem: Two homes earn the same pay. One has a high rent. Can both keep the same sum?
guided.hint: Look at what goes out first.

options.feedback: The larger bill leaves less room in one home.
Equal pay does not mean equal costs.

steps.takeaway: A saving rate is not a moral grade.

concepts.askLine: If a bill eats most of a month's pay, what could still count as a useful first step?

decoys.fix: Bills still need part of the pay before cash can stay aside.

decoys.text: judge each home by one rate,
decoys.fix: Homes face different pay and fixed bills, so room can vary.

chiku.ask: Salary day is here. What can I note before the cash goes out? Give me one card.

cards.text: Note a share that can stay
Force one rate on each home

newDay.caption: New day: a repair bill uses much of this month's spare cash.
newDay.question: Will Chiku allow the kept share to change?

guesses.why: Costs can change the cash left this month.
A fixed rate may ignore the repair bill.
Pay alone does not show what is spare.

truth.caption: Chiku notes the repair cost and a smaller spare sum.

concepts.title: Budget needs
concepts.hook: A UPI log shows tea, bus fare, rent, and a clinic bill. Which costs can move, and which cannot?
concepts.rule: Arkad's second cure sorts needs from wants. A budget can show choices, but low pay and high fixed costs leave less room than the tale suggests.

claims.text: In Seven Cures, Arkad asks his class to write down costs and rank needs before wishes.
The book says some costs can be cut. A US study says bills and low pay can block cash saved for emergencies.
SEBI advises tracking spending and putting basic needs before wants. A spending log alone cannot raise income or erase a bill.

items.stem: At a Chennai college, a student logs UPI payments. Which line is a fixed need this month?

options.feedback: The rent is due even if small daily treats are cut.

options.text: A new phone case for fun.
options.feedback: The case is a wish that can wait, unlike rent.

items.stem: A shop records each bill. Why mark food and rent apart from snacks?

options.feedback: The tale asks us to rank costs by need and value.

options.text: Each line is just a whim.
options.feedback: Food and rent are basic costs, so this label hides real needs.

items.stem: A family shop sees a big power bill in its UPI log. What may the log help it see?

options.feedback: The record makes the flow of cash plain for a review.

options.text: A new source of cash at once.
options.feedback: A log can show past costs, but it cannot create new income.

items.stem: A worker's rent and care bills rise. Which budget note is fair?

options.feedback: The bill rise can shrink spare cash even with a careful log.

options.text: The log alone will pay them.
options.feedback: Tracking is useful for sight, but cash still must cover the bills.

items.stem: A cousin calls each low saving month poor self-control. What does this miss?

options.text: Bills can take most of pay.
options.feedback: Research links thin cash buffers with fixed costs and low income.

options.text: A neat list makes rent shrink.
options.feedback: The list makes rent clear, yet the rent amount stays due.

items.stem: A budget has five cost lines: rent, food, bus fare, games, and a clinic visit. How many are basic needs?

options.feedback: Rent, food, travel, and care are basic costs in this case.
More than one cost keeps this person housed, fed, and well.

misconceptions.name: Every cost is a whim
misconceptions.correction: A budget can mark core bills apart from wants that can wait.

misconceptions.name: A log makes cash
misconceptions.correction: A record shows costs. Low pay and fixed bills may still leave little room.

steps.title: Sort the bills

hook.stem: Which cost comes before a treat?

options.feedback: Food is a core need.
The case can wait.

steps.teach: Arkad lists costs because a full purse can hide what each coin does. Food and shelter have a different role from a treat.

example.feedback: Rent keeps the home in place this month.

guided.stem: A bus ride gets a worker to the shop. How is it best marked?
guided.hint: Think of work that depends on travel.

options.feedback: The fare helps the worker reach the job.
The ride is tied to work in this case.

steps.takeaway: Mark needs before wishes.

steps.title: See the flow

hook.stem: What does a UPI log show best?

options.feedback: The list names past payments.
The list cannot show a sure future.

steps.teach: A log can show where cash went, so a home can see patterns. It does not change pay or make a bill go away.

example.feedback: The record groups cash that left in two ways.

guided.stem: A small shop lists power and stock costs. What does it gain?
guided.hint: Think of a record, not a new sale.

options.feedback: The list shows where the money went.
A list cannot promise more buyers.

steps.takeaway: A log shows costs, not new income.

steps.title: Allow for tight months

hook.stem: If rent rises, can a tidy list pay it?

options.feedback: The bill needs money, not just a note.
A record does not pay a landlord.

steps.teach: Some homes face high fixed bills, so a neat plan cannot free cash needed for food or rent.

example.feedback: A higher fixed cost can squeeze the sum left.

guided.stem: A clinic bill takes the spare cash. What is a fair reading?
guided.hint: Think of this month's real cost.

options.feedback: The care bill changed what cash was spare.
A real care need is not proof of poor care with money.

steps.takeaway: A budget cannot erase fixed costs.

decoys.fix: Food, rent, and care are core costs in many homes.

decoys.text: expect the list to make pay,
decoys.fix: A log can show the flow of cash, but it does not raise pay.

concepts.title: Growth over time
concepts.hook: Arkad lends to a shield maker, then puts the payment back to work. Why does the tale dwell on time?
concepts.rule: The third cure shows that retained earnings can add to a sum over time. The tale's high rates are an old example, not a return anyone can count on.

claims.text: In Seven Cures, Arkad lends to a shield maker and lends out the payments he gets back.
The book's coin tale shows growth on both the first sum and its past gains. Its old rate is not a promise.
A possible gain comes with risk. A person can get back less than the sum set aside.

items.stem: At a Mumbai shop, a lender gets a payment from stock sales. What did Arkad do with such cash?

options.text: He put it back to work.
options.feedback: Arkad's story has the payment join the sum that can earn again.

options.text: He called it a sure prize.
options.feedback: The tale shows his choice, but no loan comes with a sure gain.

items.stem: A worker thinks a kept rupee earns just by sitting in a purse. What is missing?

options.feedback: The purse holds cash; a gain needs some other source or deal.

options.text: A purse pays for each day.
options.feedback: Arkad says idle coins in a purse do not earn on their own.

items.stem: A Delhi family adds past gains to an FD balance. What can the next gain be based on?

options.feedback: When a gain stays in the sum, later gains can use that sum.
That leaves out the past gain which now sits in the balance.

items.stem: A long-run chart rises. Which note keeps the tale honest?

options.text: The path can vary and dip.
options.feedback: The chart is an example; real outcomes can move both ways.

options.text: The curve is a firm promise.
options.feedback: A drawn path cannot make future gains certain or safe.

items.stem: A chit fund member hears a fixed tale of fast gain. What question matters first?

options.feedback: A gain claim has to be read with its risk and terms.
A fast target can hide the chance of losing the first sum.

items.stem: For growth on past gains, a balance has ₹100 and then gains ₹10 that stays. How much can the next gain use?

options.feedback: The first sum and the gain now sit in the same balance.
That leaves out the past gain which stayed in the balance.

misconceptions.name: Growth is sure
misconceptions.correction: The tale shows a path, but gains and the first sum face risk.

misconceptions.name: Old gains do no work
misconceptions.correction: When a gain stays in the sum, later gains can draw on it too.

steps.title: Put gains back

hook.stem: What does Arkad do with a loan payment?

options.feedback: The new cash goes back to work.
The tale has him use the payment again.

steps.teach: Arkad uses a shield maker's loan payment again, so the new cash can take part in later gains. The story rests on a real borrower who pays.

parts: The gain joins the next loan.
example.spot: The gain joins the next loan.
example.feedback: This is how the story has past gain join later use.

guided.stem: A lender gets a fee back. What matches Arkad's tale?
guided.hint: Follow the cash after it comes back.

options.text: Put the fee into the next sum.
options.feedback: The fee can then share in later results.

options.text: Count the fee as the whole sum.
options.feedback: The first amount is still part of the sum.

steps.takeaway: Past gains can join the next sum.

steps.title: See time at work

hook.stem: When a gain stays, what sum is used next?

options.feedback: The gain has joined the first sum.
That skips the part which stayed.

steps.teach: A gain may add to the base, so later gains may use more than the first sum. Clason's old coin rates are an example, not a forecast.

example.feedback: The old gain is now part of the sum used next.

guided.stem: A balance grows and the gain stays. What changes?
guided.hint: Think of the sum used in the next round.

options.feedback: A kept gain adds to the balance.
Time still shapes how gains add up.

steps.takeaway: Time can add gains to gains.

steps.title: Keep risk in view

hook.stem: Can a gain plan also shrink a sum?

options.feedback: A gain is not a sure outcome.
Any plan can face risk or loss.

steps.teach: A plan can bring gain, but it can also shrink the first sum. Ask about risk because a neat old story cannot promise a result.

parts: The sum may be at risk.
example.spot: The sum may be at risk.
example.feedback: A late or missed payment can affect the first sum.

guided.stem: A friend gives a sure gain claim. What is worth checking?
guided.hint: Think of the first sum if plans go wrong.

options.feedback: The amount at stake matters as much as a gain claim.
A boast gives no clear view of risk.

steps.takeaway: Growth is a chance, not a promise.

concepts.title: Safety first
concepts.hook: A cousin offers a fast deal for saved cash. Arkad's brickmaker once brought back glass in place of jewels. What went wrong?
concepts.rule: The fourth cure asks who knows the work and how the first sum can come back. Yet no single deal is risk free; spreading risk can help.

claims.text: In Seven Cures, Arkad's first jewel deal goes wrong because he asks a brickmaker to judge jewels.
Arkad puts great weight on keeping the first sum safe. Real assets can still lose value.
Spreading a sum across different risks can reduce the harm from one bad outcome, but it cannot end all risk.

items.stem: A Delhi family shop gets a jewel tip from a trader who knows only cloth. What is the tale's warning?

options.feedback: The brickmaker knew bricks, but he could not judge jewels well.
Skill in cloth does not prove skill in jewels or their price.

items.stem: A friend knows gold prices but not a chit fund's rules. Why ask what they know?

options.feedback: Knowing one market does not grant clear sight in another one.
A warm bond is no proof that a person knows the new deal.

items.stem: A family shop puts its whole spare sum into one stock order. What can one bad sale do?

options.feedback: One shared risk can reach all the cash tied to that order.

options.text: Leave the sum safe by name.
options.feedback: Calling money spare does not stop a bad order from hurting it.

items.stem: A worker hears that a plan is safe because ten friends joined. Which question has value?

options.feedback: Many people can face the same risk from one plan.
Praise does not show how the first sum may fare.

items.stem: A seller calls a deal free of risk. Which reply fits the SEC guide?

options.text: No spread can end all risk.
options.feedback: Risk can be reduced in some cases, but it does not vanish.

options.text: A spread makes each loss nil.
options.feedback: Different holdings can still fall at the same time.

items.stem: For safety across three separate cash uses, one use goes bad. How many uses remain apart from it?

options.feedback: Two uses are apart from the one that went badly.
A bad result in one place need not reach each other place.

misconceptions.name: Skill fits all trades
misconceptions.correction: A person who knows one field may not know another deal.

misconceptions.name: One deal is safe
misconceptions.correction: Any one deal may go wrong. A spread can limit some harm, not end it.

steps.title: Check the field

hook.stem: Who can best judge a jewel?

options.feedback: That trade is the person's field.
Bricks call for a different skill.

steps.teach: Arkad's brickmaker cannot judge jewels, so a shiny deal turns bad. Skill in one trade does not grant skill in each trade.

example.feedback: That gap lets a bad purchase pass as a fine one.

guided.stem: A tailor offers to price rare coins. What needs a check?
guided.hint: Think about the kind of work.

options.feedback: Tailoring does not prove skill with rare coins.
Dress does not show coin price skill.

steps.takeaway: Match the skill to the task.

steps.title: See shared risk

hook.stem: Can one bad deal hurt a whole pot?

options.feedback: The whole pot shares that deal's risk.
A name cannot shield cash.

steps.teach: A spread can help because one bad result may touch a smaller share. It still leaves some risk when many parts move at once.

example.feedback: Three owners do not make the one cart into three risks.

guided.stem: Two shop orders rely on the same buyer. Are they apart?
guided.hint: Look for what both plans need.

options.feedback: The one buyer links both orders.
Two bills can rest on one buyer.

steps.takeaway: A spread can help when risks differ.

steps.title: Drop the sure claim

hook.stem: Does the fourth cure make loss impossible?

options.feedback: Care can help, but it is no shield from all harm.
A good check cannot stop each shock.

steps.teach: Arkad wants the first sum back, but no deal can promise that. Care and a spread may limit risk, so the book's sure tone is dated.

example.feedback: A check helps see risk, yet cannot erase it.

guided.stem: An FD is called safe. What is still worth asking?
guided.hint: Think of what may change.

options.feedback: The label alone is not the whole story.
No plan can make all risk vanish.

steps.takeaway: Care helps; certainty is too strong.

factCheck.checker: Editorial check 2026-10-27: chapter 3 and SEC diversification guide opened and read.

concepts.title: Home costs
concepts.hook: Arkad wants each family to own a roof. A renter in Bengaluru may move for work soon. What does the old cure leave out?
concepts.rule: The fifth cure praises a home of one's own. That is a dated universal rule: buying adds repair, tax, and loan costs, while renting may fit a short stay.

claims.text: In Seven Cures, Arkad urges home ownership and treats it as a way to cut living costs.
A US consumer guide says buying can add repair, tax, and moving costs that the parable plays down.
A US consumer guide says a home choice depends on length of stay, cash flow, and the risk of a price fall.

items.stem: A Bengaluru worker may shift cities next year. What cost does Arkad's home cure skip?

options.feedback: A short stay can make fees and a later move matter a lot.

options.text: The cost of a cup of tea.
options.feedback: Tea is small beside the fees tied to a home sale.

items.stem: A renter sees a low monthly loan sum. Why is that not the full home cost?

options.feedback: The loan sum leaves out bills an owner must still pay.
Owning brings real bills, even when the loan sum looks low.

items.stem: A Chennai family buys a flat and the roof leaks. What new bill can follow?

options.feedback: The owner bears repair costs that a renter may not face.
The family owns the flat, so a rent cut is no answer.

items.stem: A family wants room to move near a new job. Which housing fact matters?

options.feedback: A lease can be simpler to leave than a home to sell.
A sale and new home can bring fees and time costs.

items.stem: A friend calls rent wasted cash in each case. Which reading is fair?

options.feedback: A short stay can make the costs of buying hard to recoup.
Rent pays for a place to live and can allow a move.

items.stem: In a home cost list, count the loan, tax, and roof repair. How many cost lines are there?

options.feedback: All three are costs that may come with owning a home.
The loan is just one cost; tax and repair also count.

misconceptions.name: Owning fits each home
misconceptions.correction: A short stay and a need to move may make rent useful.

misconceptions.name: The loan is the full cost
misconceptions.correction: Tax, upkeep, and fees can sit beside the loan bill.

sources.title: The Richest Man In Babylon, chapter 3: Seven Cures for a Lean Purse

steps.title: Count the full cost

hook.stem: Does the loan bill show all owner costs?

options.feedback: Upkeep and tax can add to it.
The loan is only one line.

steps.teach: Owning adds bills because the owner pays for upkeep and tax. A low loan sum alone can hide the full cost.

parts: The owner pays to fix it.
example.spot: The owner pays to fix it.
example.feedback: The repair is a real owner cost beside the loan.

guided.stem: A flat needs new pipes. Whose cost may this be?
guided.hint: Think of who holds the flat.

options.feedback: The owner may have to pay for upkeep.
The work needs cash from someone.

steps.takeaway: Count upkeep as well as loan bills.

steps.title: Value room to move

hook.stem: Which home may be simpler to leave soon?

options.feedback: A sale can take more time and fees.

options.text: A flat that needs a sale.
options.feedback: A sale can take work and cash.

steps.teach: A rented place may fit a short stay because a home sale can cost time and fees. The choice rests on real plans.

example.feedback: Fees are part of the cost of a move.

guided.stem: A job may move next year. What is worth weighing?
guided.hint: Think of the path out of a home.

options.feedback: Both can matter for a short stay.
The shade says little about exit costs.

steps.takeaway: A short stay changes the home choice.

steps.title: Read the old cure anew

hook.stem: Does Arkad leave room for renters?

options.feedback: He urges a roof of one's own.
The cure is for owning a home.

steps.teach: Arkad praises a roof one owns, but his rule is too broad because costs and moves can make a rented home fit well.

parts: The tale likes a home deed.
example.feedback: The old cure does not fit each move or budget.

guided.stem: A friend says each renter is poorer for it. What is missing?
guided.hint: Think of cost and time in place.

options.feedback: A short stay may favor more room to move.
The sofa does not test the home cost.

steps.takeaway: Owning is a choice, not a cure for all.

concepts.title: Future needs
concepts.hook: Arkad thinks of old age and a family after an earner is gone. What kind of need sits beyond this month's UPI list?
concepts.rule: The sixth cure calls for care for later years and for dependants. A plan needs cash in reach for near shocks as well as thought for distant needs.

claims.text: In Seven Cures, Arkad asks earners to plan for old age and for the family if the earner dies.
The tale sets a far goal, but some money may need to be in reach for a sudden bill.
A US study finds that over half of US families lack cash for three months of basic costs.

items.stem: A Mumbai family lists this month's bills and a far-off care need. Which one fits Arkad's sixth cure?

options.feedback: The sixth cure asks a home to look past today's work years.
The cure looks to later life and those who may need care.

items.stem: An earner has young children. Why does Arkad look past the next pay day?

options.text: Their needs can outlast his pay.
options.feedback: The parable asks who may need support in years to come.

options.text: The next pay will cover each year.
options.feedback: One pay day cannot meet each later need by itself.

items.stem: A Delhi shop keeps cash in a place it cannot reach soon. What if the fridge breaks today?

options.text: The repair may be hard to pay.
options.feedback: Cash for a near shock has to be in reach when due.

options.text: A far plan pays at once.
options.feedback: A far-off plan may be hard to use for today's bill.

items.stem: A family has gold but little cash in reach. Which note fits the Fed study?

options.text: Value may be hard to use.
options.feedback: Wealth that is hard to use fast may not pay a near bill.

options.text: Gold makes each cash bill easy.
options.feedback: An asset can have value yet be hard to use at once.

items.stem: A cousin says later needs make today's cash buffer pointless. Which reply is sound?

options.feedback: A sudden bill and later life call for different time frames.
A bill due soon needs money that can be used soon.

items.stem: For future needs, a list has a clinic bill this week, school fees next year, and care in old age. How many time frames are on it?

options.feedback: The needs fall now, next year, and much later in life.
The list spans near and far needs, not one due date.

misconceptions.name: Only this month matters
misconceptions.correction: Family needs can last well past the next pay day.

misconceptions.name: Any asset pays a near bill
misconceptions.correction: A near shock may need cash that is easy to reach.

steps.title: Look past pay day

hook.stem: Whose needs does Arkad ask us to see?

options.feedback: He looks ahead for those who depend on pay.
The cure is about later family needs.

steps.teach: Arkad looks to old age because pay may slow while needs go on. He also asks what family may need after an earner dies.

parts: Care may be needed in old age.
example.spot: Care may be needed in old age.
example.feedback: This need is well beyond the next pay day.

guided.stem: A parent thinks of a child after work ends. Which time is in view?
guided.hint: Look past today.

options.feedback: The care need may come long after today.
The question reaches beyond today.

steps.takeaway: Later family needs deserve a place in the plan.

steps.title: Keep some cash in reach

hook.stem: What pays a sudden bus fare best?

options.text: Cash that can be used now.
options.feedback: It is ready when the fare is due.
It may be hard to use today.

steps.teach: A near bill calls for cash in reach, so value locked away may give little help today. The Fed study finds many homes lack such cash.

parts: Cash in reach pays the fare.
example.spot: Cash in reach pays the fare.
example.feedback: A payment due now needs money ready now.

guided.stem: A shop fridge breaks today. What form of money is useful?
guided.hint: Think of speed of use.

options.feedback: The repair can be paid without a long wait.
Hope is not cash for a repair bill.

steps.takeaway: Near shocks need money in reach.

steps.title: Hold two time frames

hook.stem: Can one far plan cover a bill due today?

options.feedback: The time to use the money matters.
A due date changes what can help.

concepts.title: Debt in parts
concepts.hook: Dabasir writes a plan on clay: a share to keep, a share to live on, and a share for debt. Can a fixed split fit each pay packet?
concepts.rule: The clay tablets turn a huge debt into named sums and repeat payments. The book's 10/70/20 split is an old story plan, not a rate for all homes.

claims.text: In The Clay Tablets, Dabasir divides pay: one tenth to keep, seven tenths for life, and two tenths for debts.
He names each lender and the sum owed, then records payments as his work brings cash.
A US study finds that low pay and fixed bills can block saving. Dabasir's fixed split may be hard for some homes.
